lessons.title: Understanding Steel: Carbon Content and Alloys
lessons.body: Steel is iron mixed with a small amount of carbon. The carbon content decides how hard the steel can become when heat treated. Low-carbon steel (mild steel) has less than 0.3% carbon. It is easy to forge and weld but will not harden much when quenched. You find it in rebar, car parts, and cheap angle iron. Medium-carbon steel (0.3â0.6% carbon) is a good all-rounder. It hardens enough for many tools but stays tough. Old leaf springs from trucks and cars are often 5160 steel, a medium-carbon alloy with chromium. High-carbon steel (0.6â1.5% carbon) is what you want for knives, chisels, punches, and axes. It can get very hard but also brittle if not tempered. Files, old saw blades, and coil springs are good sources. Alloy steels add other elements: chromium for wear resistance, vanadium for toughness, molybdenum for heat resistance. In Africa, you often work with recycled steel. Learn to identify it: test with a grinder â high-carbon steel throws bright yellow sparks that burst into many small forks; mild steel gives few dull orange sparks. A file test: a new file will skate over hardened high-carbon steel but bite into mild steel. When you buy steel from a scrap yard, ask for old agricultural equipment, truck axles, or plow discs â these are often medium to high carbon. Keep a few known samples in your shop for comparison. Never assume; always test. The carbon content also affects forging temperature: high-carbon steel burns at a lower temperature than mild steel, so watch your fire. With practice, you will learn to judge by feel and spark.

lessons.title: Critical Temperatures and Color Indicators
lessons.body: In blacksmithing, you judge temperature by the color of the steel in dim light. The critical temperature is where steel changes its internal structure and becomes ready for hardening. For most high-carbon steels, this is between 760Â°C and 870Â°C. In color terms, that is a bright cherry red to orange-red. A common mistake is to quench too cold. If the steel is only dull red (around 600Â°C), it will not harden. If it is bright yellow or white (over 1000Â°C), you are burning the carbon and the steel will be weak. Learn to work in a shaded area or at dusk. The colors: faint red (550Â°C) â too cold; dark cherry (650Â°C) â still too cold; cherry red (750Â°C) â starting point for hardening some steels; bright cherry (800Â°C) â good for most; orange (900Â°C) â getting hot; yellow (1000Â°C) â too hot for hardening, but okay for forging some alloys; white (1200Â°C) â burning, sparks fly. A magnet is a useful tool: steel becomes non-magnetic at its critical temperature (around 770Â°C for simple carbon steels). Heat a piece and touch it with a magnet. When it stops sticking, you are at the right temperature for quenching. This is a reliable trick in any light. For African smiths using charcoal or coal forges, the fire may be uneven. Rotate the steel to heat evenly. Use a pipe or a baffle to reduce oxygen if you are burning the steel. Always normalize after forging: heat to critical and let it cool in air. This relieves stress and refines the grain. Then you can harden. Practice with a piece of known steel until you can judge the color without a magnet. Your eyes will become your best thermometer.

lessons.title: Quenching: Oil, Water, and Air
lessons.body: Quenching is the rapid cooling of hot steel to make it hard. The speed of cooling matters: faster cooling makes harder steel but also more brittle. Water is the fastest, then oil, then air. For most simple high-carbon steels (like 1080 or 5160), oil is the best choice. Warm oil (around 50â60Â°C) cools more evenly than cold oil. You can use used motor oil, canola oil, or transmission fluid. Never use water on high-carbon steel unless you know it is a water-hardening grade (like W1). Water can crack the steel. For medium-carbon steels, oil is also good. Air-hardening steels (like A2) are rare in basic smithing; they harden by cooling in still air. But for most African workshops, oil is your friend. Set up a quench tank: a metal pipe or bucket filled with at least 4 liters of oil. The oil should be deep enough to fully submerge the tool. Heat the steel to critical (non-magnetic), then quickly plunge it into the oil. Move it around in a figure-eight motion to break the vapor barrier. Hold it under for 10â15 seconds, then pull it out. It should be cool enough to touch. If you see flames, do not panic â just cover the tank with a lid to smother the fire. Always quench point-first or edge-first for knives. For a chisel, quench the cutting end only, leaving the shank soft. This gives you a hard edge and a tough body. After quenching, test with a file. If the file skates, it is hard. If it bites, you need to reheat and quench again. Remember: safety first. Wear leather gloves, a face shield, and long sleeves. Oil can splatter and ignite. Keep a fire extinguisher or sand bucket nearby. Never quench in a plastic container â it will melt. With practice, you will learn the right speed for each steel.

lessons.title: Tempering for Toughness and Hardness
lessons.body: After quenching, steel is very hard but also brittle â it can crack or shatter like glass. Tempering removes some of that brittleness while keeping most of the hardness. You do this by heating the steel to a lower temperature (150â300Â°C) and holding it there for a while, then letting it cool slowly. The temperature you choose depends on the tool. For a knife, you want a temper around 200Â°C â this gives a good balance of hardness and toughness. For a chisel or punch, 220â250Â°C is better because it needs to withstand hammer blows. For a spring, 300Â°C makes it tough and flexible. How do you judge temperature without a thermometer? Use the oxide colors that form on clean steel as it heats. First, the steel turns pale yellow (200Â°C), then straw (220Â°C), then brown (240Â°C), then purple (280Â°C), then blue (300Â°C). These colors are your guide. Clean the steel with sandpaper or a grinder before tempering so you can see the colors clearly. Heat the steel slowly and evenly. You can use a kitchen oven, a toaster oven, or a small forge with a gentle fire. For a knife, you can also use a hot plate or even a bed of hot sand. Hold the steel at the desired color for about one hour (or two cycles of 30 minutes). Then let it cool in air. If you over-temper (go past blue), the steel becomes too soft â you will need to re-harden and re-temper. In Africa, many smiths use a charcoal fire and watch the colors carefully. It works. For a simple tool, you can temper just the cutting edge by heating the back of the tool with a torch until the edge turns the right color. This leaves the back soft and tough. Always temper after quenching. Never use a quenched tool without tempering â it will break.

lessons.title: Testing Hardness with a File
lessons.body: The file test is the simplest way to check if your steel is hard. A new, sharp file is harder than most knife steels. When you draw the file across the hardened edge, it should skate â meaning it does not bite or cut. If the file bites and removes metal, the steel is too soft. This test is not precise, but it is good enough for most blacksmithing. To do it properly: first, clean the steel with a grinder or sandpaper to remove any scale or decarburized layer. Then take a sharp file (a new one is best) and push it across the edge at a slight angle. Use light pressure. On a properly hardened and tempered knife, the file will slide with a scratching sound but not cut. On a soft piece, it will dig in and leave a shiny mark. You can also test the tip and the spine â often the spine is softer because it was not quenched or was tempered more. For a chisel, test the cutting edge. If it skates, it is hard. If it bites, re-harden and quench again. Remember that a file will also skate on work-hardened steel or on a piece that is not fully hardened but has a hard surface. So always test after grinding away a little metal. In Africa, files are common and cheap. Keep one file just for testing â mark it with tape so you do not use it for sharpening. You can also use a set of hardness testing files (like those from a machinist supply) that are calibrated to different Rockwell C scales, but they are expensive. For most smiths, a single new file is enough. Practice on known samples: a piece of mild steel will always be soft; a piece of hardened 1080 will skate. Once you know the feel, you can judge your own work. If the file skates but the edge chips, your steel is too hard â temper it more. If the file bites, it is too soft â re-harden. The file test is your daily quality control.

lessons.title: Heat Treating Simple Tools
lessons.body: Now you will heat treat three common tools: a cold chisel, a center punch, and a simple knife. For each, the process is similar but the details differ. Start with a cold chisel made from 5160 or 1080 steel. Forge the cutting edge to a 60-degree angle. Normalize: heat to cherry red and let it cool in air. Then harden: heat just the first 5 cm of the cutting end to non-magnetic (bright cherry red). Quench only that end in warm oil, moving it in a figure-eight. Hold for 10 seconds, then check with a file. It should skate. Now temper: polish the cutting end with sandpaper, then heat the shank with a torch or in the forge until the cutting edge turns straw yellow (220Â°C). Remove and cool. The edge is now hard and tough. For a center punch, use high-carbon steel. Forge a point. Harden the point by heating the tip to non-magnetic and quenching in oil. Temper to purple (280Â°C) â this makes it tough enough to take hammer blows without breaking. For a simple knife, use an old file or leaf spring. Forge the blade, then normalize three times to refine the grain. Harden the whole blade: heat to non-magnetic, quench in warm oil, edge-first. Then temper in an oven at 200Â°C for one hour. Check with a file â it should skate. If the blade warps during quenching, you can straighten it while it is still hot (around 200Â°C) using a vise or a hammer. In Africa, many smiths use a charcoal fire and a pipe to direct heat. For tempering, a charcoal fire with a bed of hot coals works â just watch the colors. Always test your tools before use. A chisel that is too hard will chip; one that is too soft will mushroom. Adjust by re-tempering or re-hardening. With practice, you will heat treat tools that last for years.

quiz.q: What is the carbon content of mild steel?
quiz.explanation: Mild steel has less than 0.3% carbon, making it easy to forge but hard to harden.

quiz.q: Which steel is best for making a knife that holds an edge?
quiz.explanation: High-carbon steel (0.6â1.5% carbon) can be hardened to hold a sharp edge.

quiz.q: What does a bright yellow spark from a grinder indicate?
quiz.explanation: High-carbon steel produces bright yellow sparks that burst into many small forks.

quiz.q: What is the critical temperature range for hardening most high-carbon steels?
quiz.explanation: Most high-carbon steels harden when heated to 760â870Â°C, which is bright cherry red to orange-red.

quiz.q: At what temperature does steel become non-magnetic?
quiz.explanation: Simple carbon steels become non-magnetic at their critical temperature, around 770Â°C.

quiz.q: Why is a magnet useful in heat treating?
options: A) It helps hold the steel
B) It indicates when the steel is at critical temperature
C) It cools the steel faster
quiz.explanation: When steel becomes non-magnetic, it has reached the right temperature for quenching.

quiz.q: What color should steel be for hardening most simple high-carbon steels?
quiz.explanation: Bright cherry red (around 800Â°C) is the correct color for hardening many high-carbon steels.

quiz.q: Which quenching medium cools steel the fastest?
quiz.explanation: Water cools steel faster than oil or air, but it can cause cracking in high-carbon steels.

quiz.q: What is the best quenching medium for most simple high-carbon steels?
quiz.explanation: Warm oil (around 50â60Â°C) cools more evenly than cold oil and is less likely to crack the steel than water.

quiz.q: Why should you move the steel in a figure-eight motion during quenching?
options: A) To make it cool faster
B) To break the vapor barrier
quiz.explanation: Moving the steel breaks the vapor barrier that forms around it, allowing faster and more even cooling.

quiz.q: What happens if you quench high-carbon steel in water?
quiz.explanation: Water cools too fast for most high-carbon steels, causing internal stresses that can lead to cracks.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of tempering?
options: B) To make steel softer and tougher
quiz.explanation: Tempering reduces brittleness and increases toughness while retaining most of the hardness.

quiz.q: What tempering color indicates approximately 200Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Pale yellow appears at around 200Â°C, which is a common tempering temperature for knives.

quiz.q: What tempering color is best for a cold chisel?
quiz.explanation: Straw (around 220Â°C) gives a good balance of hardness and toughness for a chisel.

quiz.q: What happens if you over-temper steel?
quiz.explanation: Over-tempering (going past blue) makes the steel too soft, requiring re-hardening.

quiz.q: How long should you hold a knife at tempering temperature?
quiz.explanation: Holding at tempering temperature for about one hour ensures even heating and proper tempering.

quiz.q: What is the file test used for?
quiz.explanation: A file test checks if the steel is hard enough: a sharp file will skate on hard steel and bite on soft steel.

quiz.q: What does it mean if a file skates on the steel?
options: A) The steel is too soft
C) The steel is too hot
quiz.explanation: If the file does not bite, the steel is harder than the file, indicating it is properly hardened.

quiz.q: Why should you clean the steel before the file test?
options: B) To remove scale and decarburized layer
quiz.explanation: Scale and decarburized layers can give a false reading; cleaning ensures you test the actual steel.

quiz.q: What should you do if the file bites into a hardened tool?
quiz.explanation: If the file bites, the steel is too soft, so you need to re-harden by heating and quenching again.

quiz.q: What is the first step after forging a tool before hardening?
quiz.explanation: Normalizing (heating to critical and air cooling) relieves stress and refines the grain before hardening.

quiz.q: How many times should you normalize a knife blade to refine grain?
quiz.explanation: Normalizing three times is a common practice to refine the grain structure in knife blades.

quiz.q: When hardening a cold chisel, which part do you quench?
quiz.explanation: Quenching only the cutting end leaves the shank soft and tough, reducing the risk of breakage.

quiz.q: What tempering color is suitable for a center punch?
quiz.explanation: Purple (around 280Â°C) gives the toughness needed for a punch to withstand hammer blows.

quiz.q: What can you use to temper a tool if you don't have an oven?
quiz.explanation: A charcoal fire with a gentle heat can be used to temper tools by watching the oxide colors.

quiz.q: What should you do if a knife warps during quenching?
options: B) Straighten it while still hot
quiz.explanation: Straightening while the steel is still warm (around 200Â°C) is easier and less likely to break.

quiz.q: What is the danger of using a quenched but untempered tool?
options: A) It will be too soft
B) It will break or shatter
C) It will not hold an edge
quiz.explanation: Untempered steel is very brittle and can crack or shatter under stress.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good source of high-carbon steel in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Old files are made of high-carbon steel and are commonly used by African smiths for tools.

quiz.q: What is the recommended quench oil temperature?
quiz.explanation: Warm oil at 50â60Â°C cools more evenly than cold oil and reduces the risk of cracking.

quiz.q: What should you do before testing a tool with a file after tempering?
quiz.explanation: Polishing removes oxide colors and scale so you can see the file's bite clearly.
